name: Vegetarierbund Deutschland (now ProVeg Deutschland): 2016 estimate (ACE)
summary: Promotes vegetarian and vegan eating in Germany through events, local groups, corporate and institutional outreach, labelling and media. Animal Charity Evaluators' 2016 Guesstimate model: projected costs and achievements by program, converted here by species into chicken-equivalent pain days per dollar, like our other animal models: hens spared cages as hen-years of a caged hen's suffering, other animals spared with the shared figure per animal. ACE has since stopped publishing per-dollar estimates; this is the last public one for this charity.

sections.title: Model
sections.explainer:
VEBU provided budget and accomplishments information from 2015 and estimated accomplishments information from 2016.  Estimates in this sheet are made by Animal Charity Evaluators for the full year of 2015 unless otherwise noted.

Read ACE's 2016 [review](https://animalcharityevaluators.org/research/charity-review/vebu/) of VEBU.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: charityevals adjustments on top of ACE's model.

sections.title: In chicken pain days
sections.explainer: charityevals' step, not ACE's. ACE's 2016 models count years of farmed-animal life spared, every species alike. Here hens spared cages count as years of a caged hen's suffering, and every other animal spared by the shared figure for an animal spared, split by species like a replaced meal. Each species is then counted in days of a chicken's disabling pain (Rethink Priorities' estimates); how a chicken compares with a person is the chicken slider.

Magazines and leaflets printed
rows.explainer:
ACE's 90% interval, 430K to 520K (lognormal). The best guess is its median.

VEBU provided: "VEBU publishes a quarterly lifestyle magazine for members
and subscribers
● 20,000 copies per issue"

and "In the twelve month period from Nov. 2015 to Oct. 2016 we've printed 420.000 leaflets in total (Vegan Times 'newspapers', How to go vegan leaflets, booklets, etc.). I say 'printed' and not 'handed out' because we know exactly when we print leaflets but not exactly when our local groups hand them out. As you can imagine, there is usually a delay in between. However, as our leafleting activities have been quite stable over the last years, the numbers of printed leaflets in 12 month period should be quite the same as the number of leaflets distributed in that period of time.

The 420.000 leaflets also include 23.000 vegan (bumper) stickers that have been used by our activists. Compared to a 8-page newspaper sized Vegan Times or a 16 page booklet, a sticker obviously contains way less information but as it is usally seen by way more people, my guess is that the impact of a sticker is at least the same as that of one average vegan leaflet/booklet. However, I'll leave if up to you whether you want to count those 23.000 stickers as bein equal to leaflets or not. Without the stickers, we have distributed 397.000 leaflets."

rows.label: Corporate policies influenced in 2016
rows.explainer:
ACE's 90% interval, 4 to 8 (lognormal). The best guess is its median.

VEBU provided a list of policies influenced over an indefinite period of time but emphasizing 2016, on which we found 5 policies that were definitely implemented at least in part in 2016 and would likely affect animals fairly directly (through reformulating a product to use fewer animal products or introducing plant-based options). We excluded in our count policies involving only clearer labeling, which were implemented before 2016, or which were more indirect (for example, having a specifically vegetarian display area at a food industry event).

Animals spared per leaflet
rows.explainer:
ACE's 90% interval, .21 to 1.86 (normal). The best guess is its median.

Derived from our [leafleting calculator](http://www.animalcharityevaluators.org/research/interventions/impact-calculator/). Does not include shellfish or wild fish.

As of 2011, Germans typically eat [about 75%](http://faostat3.fao.org/download/FB/CL/E) as much meat as people in the US, so since the calculator was developed from US data, we multiplied its outputs by .75.

We will treat magazines equally to leaflets; while they are longer, they have much more focus on preventing recidivism; we think there is [reason](https://www.animalcharityevaluators.org/blog/our-thoughts-on-the-cost-effectiveness-of-retention-programs/) to believe this is harder to do cost-effectively than it may appear.

The same figure is kept as shared data (Animal Charity Evaluators, under Data), which this row reads.

Meals affected per year by policies influenced in 2016
rows.explainer:
ACE's 90% interval, 200K to 8M (lognormal). The best guess is its median.

We considered the individual policies influenced by VEBU and the size of the companies involved to try to understand the likely reach of reformulated and new plant-based products. 

Not all products would take the place of a meat main course; for instance, a meal that includes vegan chocolate instead of chocolate made with milk is less impactful than a meal using a quinoa burger instead of a meat burger. In these cases we considered the approximate fraction of the animal products removed from the meal in determining the number of meals affected.

rows.label: Years of change accounted for
rows.explainer: We account for a limited term of change, because companies may revise their practices again or may have adopted the practice later without VEBU's influence. We have omitted policies that clearly lasted for less than a year or were described as trials.

rows.label: Animals spared per meal
rows.explainer: We treat one meatless meal as equivalent to between 1/3 and 1/2 of a meatless day (depending on whether breakfast is counted as a meal at which one would normally eat meat, and because we think most of the meals we're accounting for are lunches and dinners). We use the estimate of the impact of a vegetarian year originally calculated for our [online ads report](https://animalcharityevaluators.org/research/interventions/online-ads/#V). As of 2011, Germans typically eat [about 75%](http://faostat3.fao.org/download/FB/CL/E) as much meat as people in the US, so since the report was developed from US data, we multiplied its outputs by .75.

Social Media proportion of programs
Social Media cost ($)
Views of content related to VEBU through the media
rows.explainer:
ACE's 90% interval, 6M to 150M (lognormal). The best guess is its median.

VEBU told us they reach an estimated 284.4 million people through year through print media.

Charities typically receive these numbers through media reporting services, which we don't understand well and which are likely to at least sometimes over-report views. Charities have told us that they have spoken to multiple media reporting services who acknowledge that these numbers are likely too high, as they are often based off of views of a newspaper or television program in total, rather than of the specific content of interest. However, we report them because there are also factors that make it seem plausible that they are at least broadly right:

* Media and advertisers have strong financial interests in knowing how many people view each type of content produced, and a long history of developing methods for tracking these numbers. The amount of media that is now viewed online makes this easier.
* Many people encounter the same news story through multiple outlets on or around the day that it breaks, or multiple times through the same outlet (e.g. on both the morning and evening news shows, in the newspaper and on TV, through Facebook friends sharing different reporting about the same event). We expect these people are counted once for each time they see a related story.

We don't use this value in further calculations because VEBU has told us that the content they are referring to here is mostly aimed at normalizing vegetarianism and is very different from the content associated with online ads programs and others which we might otherwise compare media views to.

rows.label: SADs averted per animal spared
rows.explainer: The shared figures for a replaced meal, in suffering-adjusted days (SADs) and in animals, give the suffering behind each animal spared: about 8.7 SADs. Every model that counts animals spared uses this one rate, split by species. ACE's 2016 sheets don't give a species breakdown, so the split is ACE's 2024 estimate of which animals a plant-based diet spares.

rows.label: Chicken-equivalent pain days averted per dollar you give: chickens
rows.explainer: The SADs for chickens with Ambitious Impact's weight for a hen (46% of a person's) taken out, which leaves days of a chicken's disabling pain. A chicken counts as 1 here by definition; how a chicken's suffering compares with a person's is the chicken slider. The evaluator view keeps Ambitious Impact's weight, so ACE's own result reproduces.
